POSTNUPTIAL AGREEMENT
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF EXISTING MARRIAGE
This Postnuptial Agreement is entered into on September 1, 2026 by and between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, who were married to each other on June 14, 2015 and remain married as of the date of this Agreement. Unlike a premarital agreement, which is entered into in contemplation of marriage and becomes effective upon marriage, this Agreement is entered into during an existing marriage and, unless otherwise stated in this Agreement, is intended to take effect immediately upon signing.

INTERSPOUSAL FIDUCIARY DUTY
In transactions between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, California law subjects spouses to the general rules governing fiduciary relationships that control persons in confidential relations with each other, including a duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing, a bar on either spouse taking unfair advantage of the other, and — as to community property — an obligation to give the other spouse access to books kept regarding a transaction, to render true and full information affecting a transaction on request, and to account for and hold as trustee any benefit or profit derived from a transaction made without the other spouse's consent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) Except as provided in Sections 143, 144, 146, 16040, 16047, and 21385 of the Probate Code, in transactions between themselves, spouses are subject to the general rules governing fiduciary relationships that control the actions of persons occupying confidential relations with each other. This confidential relationship imposes a duty of the highest good faith and fair dealing on each spouse, and neither shall take any unfair advantage of the other. This confidential relationship is a fiduciary relationship subject to the same rights and duties of nonmarital business partners, as provided in Sections 16403, 16404, and 16503 of the Corporations Code, including, but not limited to, the following: (1) Providing each spouse access at all times to any books kept regarding a transaction for the purposes of inspection and copying. (2) Rendering upon request, true and full information of all things affecting any transaction that concerns the community property. Nothing in this section is intended to impose a duty for either spouse to keep detailed books and records of community property transactions. (3) Accounting to the spouse, and holding as a trustee, any benefit or profit derived from any transaction by one spouse without the consent of the other spouse that concerns the community property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 721(b) (California Legislative Information text), the interspousal fiduciary duty and its specific obligations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=721.)
  Known gap: This is California's interspousal fiduciary-duty statute, used as real evidence of what a "confidential relationship" duty between spouses consists of under one state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement. California is a community-property state; most U.S. states use common-law/equitable-distribution property systems instead, and this duty framework is tied specifically to California's community-property structure. Separately: § 721 itself, read in full, does not contain the word "presumption" or state a burden-shifting rule for transactions that advantage one spouse — any such presumption is judicial doctrine, not statutory text, and no statutory citation is offered for it here. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 721(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

DEFAULT COMMUNITY AND SEPARATE PROPERTY CHARACTERIZATION
Absent an agreement changing these defaults, California law characterizes property acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in California as community property. Separate property, by contrast, includes property owned before marriage, property acquired during marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent, and the rents, issues, and profits of that separate property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Except as otherwise provided by statute, all property, real or personal, wherever situated, acquired by a married person during the marriage while domiciled in this state is community property."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 760 (California Legislative Information text), the community property default (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=760.)
  "(a) Separate property of a married person includes all of the following: (1) All property owned by the person before marriage. (2) All property acquired by the person after marriage by gift, bequest, devise, or descent. (3) The rents, issues, and profits of the property described in this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 770(a) (California Legislative Information text), the separate property definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=770.)
  Known gap: These are California's default property-characterization statutes, used as real evidence of the specific default rules a California postnuptial agreement would exist to override — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement. Community property is itself a minority approach among U.S. states; most states are common-law/equitable-distribution states, where property acquired during marriage is not automatically split into "community" and "separate" categories in this way, and a postnuptial agreement drafted for a non-community-property state would be overriding a different set of default rules entirely.

TRANSMUTATION WRITING / EXPRESS DECLARATION REQUIREMENT
California law permits married persons to change ("transmute") the character of property between community and separate, or between the spouses, by agreement or transfer, with or without consideration. Such a change of character is not valid unless made in writing by an express declaration that is made, joined in, consented to, or accepted by the spouse whose interest in the property is adversely affected.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Subject to Sections 851 to 853, inclusive, married persons may by agreement or transfer, with or without consideration, do any of the following: (a) Transmute community property to separate property of either spouse. (b) Transmute separate property of either spouse to community property. (c) Transmute separate property of one spouse to separate property of the other spouse."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 850 (California Legislative Information text), the transmutation authorization (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=850.)
  "(a) A transmutation of real or personal property is not valid unless made in writing by an express declaration that is made, joined in, consented to, or accepted by the spouse whose interest in the property is adversely affected."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 852(a) (California Legislative Information text), the writing/express declaration requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=852.)
  Known gap: This is California's transmutation statute, used as real evidence of one state's formal-validity rule for changing property character between spouses — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement. Community property (and its transmutation concept) is itself a minority framework among U.S. states; most states use common-law/equitable-distribution systems that do not use "transmutation" as a legal category at all. Separately, California courts have required specific, unambiguous language to satisfy the "express declaration" standard, but the statutory text itself does not spell out a required form of words beyond "express declaration... adversely affected" — that further specificity is judicial interpretation, not quoted here as statutory text.

PERSONAL-GIFT EXCEPTION TO THE WRITING REQUIREMENT
California's writing/express-declaration requirement for transmutations does not apply to a gift between spouses of clothing, wearing apparel, jewelry, or other tangible articles of a personal nature that is used solely or principally by the spouse receiving the gift, provided the gift is not substantial in value taking into account the circumstances of the marriage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(c) This section does not apply to a gift between the spouses of clothing, wearing apparel, jewelry, or other tangible articles of a personal nature that is used solely or principally by the spouse to whom the gift is made and that is not substantial in value taking into account the circumstances of the marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 852(c) (California Legislative Information text), the personal-gift exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=852.)
  Known gap: This is a specific statutory carve-out within California's transmutation statute, used as real evidence that at least one state's transmutation-writing rule has a bounded gift exception — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement, and not a claim about what dollar or value threshold counts as "substantial" (the statute does not itself define that term numerically). Community property is a minority approach among U.S. states. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 852(c)); no additional independent source was found for this.

RECORDING AND THIRD-PARTY EFFECT OF A REAL PROPERTY TRANSMUTATION
Under California's transmutation statute, a transmutation of real property is not effective as to third parties without notice of it unless the transmutation instrument is recorded. This recording rule addresses effectiveness against third parties; it is a separate concept from the writing/express-declaration requirement that governs validity of the transmutation as between the spouses themselves.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) A transmutation of real property is not effective as to third parties without notice thereof unless recorded."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 852(b) (California Legislative Information text), the third-party recording rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=852.)
  Known gap: This is California's transmutation statute, used as real evidence of one state's third-party recording rule for a real-property transmutation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement, and not a claim that recording is required for the transmutation to be valid between the spouses themselves (the statute ties recording only to effect on third parties without notice). Community property is a minority approach among U.S. states, and a non-community-property state's recording/title rules for interspousal real property transfers may differ materially. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 852(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

PROPERTY SCHEDULE AND EXPRESS DECLARATION
Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee identify the property listed in the attached property schedule and, as to each item so listed, expressly declare the character of that property (community property, separate property of Jordan Alex Lee, or separate property of Morgan Casey Lee) as stated in the schedule. Each party joins in, consents to, and accepts the characterization stated for each item as to that party's interest in the item. ☐ Property schedule attached.

COMMUNITY PROPERTY MANAGEMENT, GIFTS, AND DISCLOSURE DUTY
Beyond the general interspousal fiduciary duty, California's community-property management statute states that a spouse may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of it for less than fair and reasonable value, without the other spouse's written consent — except that this rule does not apply to gifts one spouse gives directly to the other. The same statute also restates a full-disclosure obligation: each spouse must make full disclosure to the other of all material facts and information regarding the existence, characterization, and valuation of community assets and debts, and provide equal access to related information, records, and books on request.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(b) A spouse may not make a gift of community personal property, or dispose of community personal property for less than fair and reasonable value, without the written consent of the other spouse. This subdivision does not apply to gifts mutually given by both spouses to third parties and to gifts given by one spouse to the other spouse."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1100(b) (California Legislative Information text), the written-consent-for-gifts rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1100.)
  "(e) Each spouse shall act with respect to the other spouse in the management and control of the community assets and liabilities in accordance with the general rules governing fiduciary relationships which control the actions of persons having relationships of personal confidence as specified in Section 721, until such time as the assets and liabilities have been divided by the parties or by a court. This duty includes the obligation to make full disclosure to the other spouse of all material facts and information regarding the existence, characterization, and valuation of all assets in which the community has or may have an interest and debts for which the community is or may be liable, and to provide equal access to all information, records, and books that pertain to the value and character of those assets and debts, upon request."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1100(e) (California Legislative Information text), the restated disclosure duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1100.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 1100, subdivisions (b) and (e)); no additional independent source was found for this beyond that one section — it is used as real evidence of a specific written-consent-for-gifts rule and a restated disclosure duty under one state's community-property management statute, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement. Community property is a minority framework among U.S. states.

SPOUSAL SUPPORT TERMS — STATUTORY BASIS DIFFERS FROM A PREMARITAL AGREEMENT
California's Uniform Premarital Agreement Act defines a "premarital agreement" as an agreement between prospective spouses made in contemplation of marriage and effective upon marriage. That Act's specific spousal-support-waiver conditions — independent counsel and non-unconscionability at enforcement — are stated as conditions on a "premarital agreement," by that definition. An agreement addressing spousal support entered into by people who are already married is not a "premarital agreement" under that definition; its validity is instead a function of the general interspousal fiduciary duty and transmutation rules described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“Premarital agreement” means an agreement between prospective spouses made in contemplation of marriage and to be effective upon marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1610(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of a premarital agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1610.)
  "(c) Any provision in a premarital agreement regarding spousal support, including, but not limited to, a waiver of it, is not enforceable if the party against whom enforcement of the spousal support provision is sought was not represented by independent counsel at the time the agreement containing the provision was signed, or if the provision regarding spousal support is unconscionable at the time of enforcement. An otherwise unenforceable provision in a premarital agreement regarding spousal support may not become enforceable solely because the party against whom enforcement is sought was represented by independent counsel."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 1612(c) (California Legislative Information text), the spousal-support-waiver conditions, tied to a premarital agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=1612.)
  Known gap: This is California's statutory definition of "premarital agreement" and its spousal-support-waiver conditions, used as real evidence that one state's specific independent-counsel/unconscionability conditions for spousal-support waivers are, by the statute's own terms, tied to agreements made before marriage — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement, and not a claim that identical or similar conditions do or do not apply to a postnuptial spousal-support provision under California law generally. No statutory text extending § 1612(c)'s specific conditions to agreements entered into after marriage was located in the sections researched for this document; that gap is disclosed rather than assumed.

TRANSMUTATION'S INTERACTION WITH A WILL AND NONPROBATE TRANSFERS
California's transmutation statute addresses two specific death-related scenarios. A statement in a will about the character of property is not admissible as evidence of a transmutation in a proceeding commenced before the death of the person who made the will. Separately, a written joinder or written consent to a nonprobate transfer of community property on death that satisfies the transmutation writing requirement is itself treated as a transmutation, governed by transmutation law rather than the Probate Code's nonprobate-transfer provisions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) A statement in a will of the character of property is not admissible as evidence of a transmutation of the property in a proceeding commenced before the death of the person who made the will."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 853(a) (California Legislative Information text), a will statement isn't evidence of transmutation before death (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=853.)
  "(c) A written joinder or written consent to a nonprobate transfer of community property on death that satisfies Section 852 is a transmutation and is governed by the law applicable to transmutations and not by Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 of Division 5 of the Probate Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 853(c) (California Legislative Information text), written consent to a nonprobate transfer is itself a transmutation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=853.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 853, subdivisions (a) and (c)); no additional independent source was found for this beyond that one section — it is used as real evidence of two specific, narrow statutory rules connecting transmutation to death-related proceedings under one state's law, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement, and not a claim that transmutation law generally displaces probate or divorce proceedings beyond what these two subdivisions state. Beyond these two rules, this document's research did not find a separate statutory mechanism for how a transmuted property's new character carries into probate or dissolution proceedings — the working assumption, not independently verified as a distinct statutory rule, is that reclassified property is simply treated according to its new character (separate or community) like any other property of that character. Community property is a minority approach among U.S. states.

SIGNATURES, ACKNOWLEDGMENT, AND RECORDING REFERENCE
This Agreement is signed by Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee below and acknowledged before a notary public. If this Agreement changes the character of any item of real property, a memorandum or the instrument itself referencing that change may be recorded in the county where the real property is located; recording affects whether the change is effective as to third parties without notice of it, and is a separate matter from the validity of the change as between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee themselves.

Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Morgan Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

citations.quote: (c) A written joinder or written consent to a nonprobate transfer of community property on death that satisfies Section 852 is a transmutation and is governed by the law applicable to transmutations and not by Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 of Division 5 of the Probate Code.

expectedJSON.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 853, subdivisions (a) and (c)); no additional independent source was found for this beyond that one section — it is used as real evidence of two specific, narrow statutory rules connecting transmutation to death-related proceedings under one state's law, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific postnuptial agreement, and not a claim that transmutation law generally displaces probate or divorce proceedings beyond what these two subdivisions state. Beyond these two rules, this document's research did not find a separate statutory mechanism for how a transmuted property's new character carries into probate or dissolution proceedings — the working assumption, not independently verified as a distinct statutory rule, is that reclassified property is simply treated according to its new character (separate or community) like any other property of that character. Community property is a minority approach among U.S. states.
